crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 2.1 The prediction function is the model
text:
2.1 The prediction function is the model
When we write
\[
\hat{y}_i = f(x_i),
\]
we are saying:

\(x_i\) is the input for observation \(i\)
\(f\) is the rule we use
\(\hat{y}_i\) is the output produced by that rule

So the prediction function is simply the model itself.
This is one of the most important identifications in machine learning:
the model is a function.
Not a vague idea. Not a black box in a philosophical sense!! Mathematically, it is a function.
It takes something in and returns something out.
So whenever someone says:

“fit a model”
“train a model”
“use the model to predict”

what they really mean is:
find a useful function \(f\), then apply it to new inputs.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 2.2 Input goes in, prediction comes out
text:
2.2 Input goes in, prediction comes out
Let us write the input more explicitly.
Usually,
\[
x_i = (x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \dots, x_{ip})
\]
This means observation \(i\) has \(p\) features.
For example, if we are predicting disease risk, then maybe
\[
x_i = (\text{age}, \text{BMI}, \text{protein}_1, \text{protein}_2, \dots, \text{protein}_{100})
\]
The prediction function takes this whole vector as input:
\[
f(x_i) = f(x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \dots, x_{ip})
\]
and returns one number:
\[
\hat{y}_i
\]
So the model does not usually look at one feature alone. It looks at the whole collection of features together.
This is important, because later tree models will make decisions based on one feature at a time at each split, but the full prediction still depends on the full path through the tree, which depends on the full input vector.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 2.3 A function can be simple or complicated
text:
2.3 A function can be simple or complicated
A prediction function can take many forms.
Some are very simple.
Some are very flexible.
Some are easy to interpret.
Some are extremely powerful but harder to understand directly.
The key point is that all of them are still functions.
For example, all of the following are prediction functions:

A constant model
\[
f(x) = 7
\]
This ignores the input completely and always predicts 7.


A linear model
\[
f(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p
\]
This predicts by adding weighted features together.


A tree model
A tree does not usually have one compact formula like a linear model. Instead, it looks more like:

if \(x_1 < 3.2\), go left
otherwise go right
then ask another question
finally assign a leaf score

So it is still a function, but it is defined by rules rather than one smooth formula.


A neural network
A neural network is also a function. It just has many nested layers and many parameters.
So the central message is:
machine learning models can look very different, but mathematically they are all just functions that map inputs to predictions.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 2.4 What does the function output actually mean?
text:
2.4 What does the function output actually mean?
This depends on the problem.
The output of the prediction function is not always interpreted in the same way.

In regression
The output is usually the final predicted quantity itself.
For example,
\[
\hat{y}_i = 182.4
\]
might mean predicted predicted glucose level or predicted gene abundance.


In binary classification
The output is often not the final class directly.
Instead, the model may first output a score:
\[
f(x_i) = 1.7
\]
Then we may transform that score into a probability, for example using the logistic function:
\[
p_i = \frac{1}{1+e^{-f(x_i)}}
\]
If this probability is above some threshold, we predict class 1; otherwise class 0.
So in many classification models, the prediction function first gives a raw score, not a probability and not a class label.
This becomes very important in XGBoost, because XGBoost often builds and updates these raw scores directly.


In ranking
The output may simply be a ranking score. The exact value may not matter by itself. What matters is whether higher-scored items are placed above lower-scored items.
So the same notation
\[
\hat{y}_i = f(x_i)
\]
can mean different things depending on the task.
That is why loss functions later become so important: they tell us what kind of output behavior we actually want.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 2.5 A model family versus one specific model
text:
2.5 A model family versus one specific model
Now we need an important distinction.
When we say “linear model,” we usually do not mean one exact fixed function. We mean a whole family of possible functions.
For example, the linear model family is
\[
f(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p
\]
But unless we know the values of \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_p\), we do not yet have one specific model.
We only have a model form.
This is a huge idea.
A model family tells us the shape of the function.
The parameters tell us the exact member of that family.
So we should distinguish between:

Model family
The set of all functions of a certain type.


Specific fitted model
One chosen function inside that family.
For example:

“all straight lines” is a family
one exact line with slope 2 and intercept 5 is one fitted model

Later in XGBoost:

the family will be all tree ensembles of a certain kind
training will choose one particular ensemble from that family
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
text:
2.6 What are parameters?
Parameters are the unknown parts of the model that must be learned from data.
In a linear model,
\[
f(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p
\]
the parameters are the coefficients
\[
\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_p
\]
Before training, we do not know them.
After training, we estimate them from data.
In a tree, the parameters are different. They include things like:

which variable to split on
where to split
what score each leaf should output

In XGBoost, the “parameters” are even richer. They include the structures of many trees and the leaf scores inside them.
So parameters are not always simple numbers like slopes. They are whatever parts of the model must be learned.
This is why tree learning is harder than ordinary linear regression. In linear regression, the structure is fixed and we only estimate coefficients. In tree models, even the structure itself is unknown.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
text:
2.7 Parameters are not predictions
This sounds obvious, but we often mix them up.
Let us separate three things very clearly:

Inputs
\[
x_i
\]
These are the observed features.


Parameters
For example, \[
\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_p
\]
or, in a tree, split points and leaf scores.
These are the unknown internal quantities we learn.


Predictions
\[
\hat{y}_i = f(x_i)
\]
These are the outputs after the input has been passed through the model.
So the usual flow is:

choose a model form

estimate the parameters from training data

plug an input into the fitted function

get a prediction

This separation is essential.
Later in XGBoost, we might confuse:

leaf score
gradient
prediction
probability

These are not the same thing. So it is worth building the habit now of keeping model pieces separate.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
text:
2.8 Examples of prediction functions
Let us walk through a few concrete cases.

Example 1: constant model
Suppose
\[
f(x) = 10
\]
Then no matter what the input is, the output is always 10.
This is a terrible model for most real tasks, but it is still a valid prediction function.


Example 2: one-feature linear model
Suppose
\[
f(x) = 2 + 3x
\]
If the input is \(x=4\), then
\[
\hat{y} = 2 + 3(4) = 14
\]
Here the function is very explicit and easy to compute.


Example 3: two-feature linear model
Suppose
\[
f(x_1,x_2) = 1 + 2x_1 - 0.5x_2
\]
If a person has \(x_1=3\) and \(x_2=8\), then
\[
\hat{y} = 1 + 2(3) - 0.5(8) = 1 + 6 - 4 = 3
\]


Example 4: tree model
Suppose the rule is:

if age < 50, predict 0.2
if age \(\geq 50\) and BMI < 30, predict 0.6
if age \(\geq 50\) and BMI \(\geq 30\), predict 1.1

This is also a prediction function.
It is not written as one algebraic line, but it is still a mapping from input to output.
That is why trees fit naturally into the supervised learning framework :)
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 2.9 The same input can be modeled in different ways
text:
2.9 The same input can be modeled in different ways
This is another central idea.
The same dataset can be modeled by many different function classes.
For the same input vector \(x_i\), we could use:

a linear regression model
a logistic regression model
a single tree
a random forest
an XGBoost ensemble
a neural network

So the question in machine learning is not only:
what is the data?
It is also:
what family of functions is suitable for that data?
For example:

if the relationship is close to linear, linear models may work very well
if there are nonlinear thresholds and interactions, trees may work better
if the pattern is very complex, ensembles may work better than one simple model

XGBoost becomes interesting because it uses many trees added together, which creates a much more flexible function than one single tree.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
text:
2.10 Why trees are functions too
We are often comfortable with formulas like
\[
f(x)=\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2
\]
but feel that a tree is somehow different.
It is different in representation, but not in mathematical role.
A function is simply a rule that assigns one output to each input.
A tree does exactly that.
Give the tree an input vector \(x\). The input moves through a sequence of decisions. Eventually it lands in one leaf. That leaf returns a score.
So a tree is a function:
\[
f(x) = \text{leaf score assigned to } x
\]
Later XGBoost writes this more formally as
\[
f(x)=w_{q(x)}
\]
where:

\(q(x)\) tells us which leaf the observation goes to
\(w\) stores the score of each leaf

This may look strange at first, but it is just a compact way of saying:
find the leaf for this observation, then return that leaf’s value.
So even though trees look algorithmic, they are still perfectly valid mathematical functions.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 2.11 Why the function matters more than the algorithm at first
text:
2.11 Why the function matters more than the algorithm at first
We should first separate the prediction function from the algorithm used to find it.
For example, in linear regression:

the function family is linear
the algorithm might be least squares

In XGBoost:

the function family is tree ensembles
the algorithm is additive boosting with gradient and Hessian based optimization

This distinction matters a lot. Because two methods can use the same function family but different training algorithms.
A major example is:

random forest
gradient boosting

Both use ensembles of trees.
So from the viewpoint of prediction function, they are closely related.
The big difference is not the type of final object only. The big difference is how the trees are learned.
This is exactly why the XGBoost tutorial says random forest and boosted trees are really the same model family in an important sense.
We will return to this later in detail.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 2.12 The function is fixed only after training
text:
2.12 The function is fixed only after training
Before training, we usually do not know the exact function. We only know the form we are willing to consider. So before training, we might say:
“We are going to search among all tree ensembles of a certain kind.” After training, we end up with one specific fitted function. So learning is the process of moving from a broad family of possible functions to one chosen function that seems to predict well. That is why training is really a search or optimization problem. We do not invent the final function manually. We define a space of possible functions, then let the training procedure choose one.
This is a very important thing for the next section on the objective function. Because once we say we are searching for the best function, the next question becomes:
best according to what?
That question leads directly to loss functions and regularization.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
text:
2.13 A useful mental picture
At this point, at this point i would like you to imagine the following.
We have a box called \(f\).
We feed in the features:
\[
x_i = (x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \dots, x_{ip})
\]
and the box returns a number:
\[
\hat{y}_i = f(x_i)
\]
Different model classes build this box differently:

linear model: weighted sum
tree: sequence of splits leading to a leaf
XGBoost: sum of many trees

So the entire rest of the chapter is really about two questions:

what kind of function should we use?

how do we learn that function from data?

We first said why we need such a function at all and clarified what the function is.
The next step is to ask:
how do we decide whether one function is better than another? That takes us directly to the idea of the objective function.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 3.1 Learning means choosing among many possible functions
text:
3.1 Learning means choosing among many possible functions
Suppose we have a dataset
\[
(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \dots, (x_n, y_n).
\]
We also choose a model family. For example:

all linear models
all decision trees
all tree ensembles
all neural networks of a certain form

That means we are not searching over all imaginable functions in the universe. We are searching inside a chosen family of possible functions.
So the learning problem becomes:
among all functions in our chosen family, find one that predicts well.
This is already a big simplification. We are essentially asking: which allowed function gives the best predictions according to our chosen rule?
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 3.2 We need a way to measure “good”
text:
3.2 We need a way to measure “good”
The phrase “predicts well” sounds natural, but mathematically it is too vague.
We need to make it measurable.
If one model predicts 10.2 and the true value is 10.0, while another predicts 18.7, then clearly the first is better. But we need a formal rule that says this.
That rule is called a loss function.
A loss function tells us how bad a prediction is.
For one observation, we write it as
\[
l(y_i, \hat{y}_i) = l(y_i, f(x_i)).
\]
This means:

\(y_i\) is the true answer
\(\hat{y}_i = f(x_i)\) is the prediction
\(l(y_i, \hat{y}_i)\) measures the penalty for being wrong

So learning becomes possible only after we define what “wrong” means.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
text:
3.3 Loss for one observation
Let us start with one single data point.
Suppose the true value is
\[
y_i = 7
\]
and our model predicts
\[
\hat{y}_i = 5.
\]
Then the prediction error is 2 in magnitude.
One simple way to measure this is squared error:
\[
l(y_i, \hat{y}_i) = (y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2.
\]
In this case,
\[
(7 - 5)^2 = 4.
\]
If instead the model predicted 6.5, then the loss would be
\[
(7 - 6.5)^2 = 0.25.
\]
So smaller loss means better prediction.
That is the whole point.
The loss turns prediction quality into a number we can optimize.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 3.4 From one observation to the full dataset
text:
3.4 From one observation to the full dataset
Of course, we do not care about only one observation. We care about all training observations together.
So we add the losses across all samples:
\[
L(f) = \sum_{i=1}^n l(y_i, f(x_i)).
\]
This is the total training loss.
It tells us how badly the model performs on the training data as a whole.
If we use squared error, then
\[
L(f) = \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - f(x_i))^2.
\]
So now we finally have something that can be minimized.
A function with smaller total loss fits the training data better.
This is the first major step in turning learning into mathematics.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
text:
3.5 Learning as optimization
Now we can express learning in a very compact way.
We want to find the function \(f\) that minimizes total loss:
\[
f^\ast = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \sum_{i=1}^n l(y_i, f(x_i)),
\]
where \(\mathcal{F}\) is the family of allowed functions.
This expression is extremely important.
Let us unpack it carefully.

\(\mathcal{F}\)
This is the model family. It is the set of functions we allow ourselves to search over.


\(\sum_{i=1}^n l(y_i, f(x_i))\)
This is the total loss on the training data.


\(\arg\min\)
This means: find the function \(f\) that gives the smallest value of that total loss.
So learning is basically optimization.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 3.6 Why learning is not just “fit the data as closely as possible”
text:
3.6 Why learning is not just “fit the data as closely as possible”
At this point, it may seem that the story is complete:

define a loss
minimize it
done

But if that were enough, machine learning would be much easier than it really is.
The problem is that minimizing training loss alone can lead to overfitting.
A very flexible model can often fit training data extremely well, even if much of what it fits is just noise.
So a model can have:

very low training loss
very poor future performance

This is one of the central problems in statistical learning. It means that “best fit on training data” is not always the same as “best model for prediction on new data.”
That is why we need one more ingredient.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 3.7 Learning should reward fit but penalize unnecessary complexity
text:
3.7 Learning should reward fit but penalize unnecessary complexity
Suppose two models fit the training data almost equally well.

one is simple and smooth
the other is highly wiggly and complicated



Code
set.seed(123)

# Simulated data
x <- seq(0, 10, length.out = 40)
y_true <- sin(x / 1.5)
y <- y_true + rnorm(length(x), sd = 0.25)

# Smooth/simple fit
fit_simple <- smooth.spline(x, y, spar = 0.8)

# Wiggly/complex fit
fit_complex <- smooth.spline(x, y, spar = 0.2)

# Fine grid for drawing curves
x_grid <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 400)
pred_simple <- predict(fit_simple, x_grid)$y
pred_complex <- predict(fit_complex, x_grid)$y

# Side-by-side plots
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))

# Plot 1: simple model
plot(x, y,
     pch = 16,
     xlab = "x",
     ylab = "y",
     main = "Simple model",
     cex = 0.9)
lines(x_grid, sin(x_grid / 1.5), lty = 2, lwd = 2)
lines(x_grid, pred_simple, lwd = 3)

mtext("Good fit, low complexity", side = 3, line = 0.2, cex = 0.9)

# Plot 2: complex model
plot(x, y,
     pch = 16,
     xlab = "x",
     ylab = "y",
     main = "Complicated model",
     cex = 0.9)
lines(x_grid, sin(x_grid / 1.5), lty = 2, lwd = 2)
lines(x_grid, pred_complex, lwd = 3)

mtext("Similar fit, higher complexity", side = 3, line = 0.2, cex = 0.9)









Usually, the simpler one is safer. Why? Because the complicated one may be reacting to accidental noise.
So in practice, we do not want to reward fit alone. We also want to control complexity.
This leads to the idea of regularization.
Instead of minimizing only training loss, we minimize:
\[
\text{Objective} = \text{Training Loss} + \text{Complexity Penalty}.
\]
In symbols,
\[
\text{obj}(f) = L(f) + \Omega(f),
\]
where:

\(L(f)\) measures fit to training data
\(\Omega(f)\) measures model complexity

This idea becomes absolutely central in XGBoost.
In fact, one reason XGBoost is so powerful is that it writes the tree learning problem explicitly in this form.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 3.8 Why regularization belongs inside learning, not as an afterthought
text:
3.8 Why regularization belongs inside learning, not as an afterthought
Some think of regularization as a side trick added later to stop models from becoming too wild.
That is not the right way to think about it. Regularization is part of the learning problem itself. Because the real goal is not to fit the observed data as tightly as possible but to learn a function that captures the true pattern and generalizes to new data.
That means a model should be judged not only by how closely it fits, but also by how believable and stable that fit is.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
text:
3.9 Training is a search problem
Once we define an objective, learning becomes a search problem.
We are searching for the function in our model family that makes the objective as small as possible.
This search may be easy or hard depending on the model class.

In linear regression
The search is relatively easy. There is a closed-form solution in ordinary least squares.


In neural networks
The search is much harder. We usually rely on iterative gradient-based optimization.


In trees
The search is also hard, but in a different way. The challenge is not only numeric parameters. The structure itself is unknown.
We must decide:

which variable to split on
where to split
how deep the tree should be
what each leaf should predict

That is why tree learning is a combinatorial optimization problem, not just a smooth calculus problem.
This will later explain why XGBoost uses clever approximations and greedy procedures.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 3.10 Why we cannot usually test every possible model
text:
3.10 Why we cannot usually test every possible model
In theory, learning sounds simple:

write down all possible models in the family

compute the objective for each one

choose the best

But in practice, that is impossible for most useful model families.
Even for trees, the number of possible structures becomes enormous very quickly.
So in real machine learning, learning usually means finding a very good solution, even if we cannot check all possible solutions exactly.
This is a very important practical idea. The optimization problem is often too large to solve perfectly. So machine learning algorithms are usually intelligent approximation procedures.
XGBoost is exactly such a procedure.
It does not search all possible ensembles of trees. Instead, it adds one tree at a time and optimizes each step carefully.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 3.11 Learning is about updating the model based on mistakes
text:
3.11 Learning is about updating the model based on mistakes
There is also an intuitive way to think about learning.
A model makes predictions. We compare them with the truth. Where the model is wrong, it should be adjusted.
So learning is a repeated cycle:

predict

measure error

adjust the model to reduce the error

This simple cycle is behind many machine learning methods.
In linear regression, the adjustment may be solved directly.
In gradient methods, we use derivatives to understand how to change the model.
In boosting, we repeatedly add new functions that correct the current model’s mistakes.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
section: 3.12 A small example: choosing between two functions
text:
3.12 A small example: choosing between two functions
Suppose we have three observations:
\[
(1,2), \quad (2,4), \quad (3,6)
\]
and we are considering two possible functions:
\[
f_1(x)=2x
\]
and
\[
f_2(x)=x+1.
\]
Let us evaluate them with squared error.

For \(f_1(x)=2x\)
Predictions are:
\[
2,\ 4,\ 6
\]
which match the true values exactly.
So total loss is
\[
(2-2)^2 + (4-4)^2 + (6-6)^2 = 0.
\]


For \(f_2(x)=x+1\)
Predictions are:
\[
2,\ 3,\ 4
\]
So total loss is
\[
(2-2)^2 + (4-3)^2 + (6-4)^2 = 0 + 1 + 4 = 5.
\]
So based on this loss, \(f_1\) is better.
This is a tiny toy example, but it captures the whole logic:

define candidate functions
compute a loss
choose the better one

Real machine learning is this same logic on much larger and more complex spaces.
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
text:
3.13 The role of the algorithm
It is useful to separate two questions:

Statistical question
What objective should define a good model?


Computational question
How do we actually find a model that minimizes that objective?
These are related, but not the same.
For example, two methods might optimize the same general type of objective but use different algorithms.
Or two methods might use similar algorithms but define different losses.
In XGBoost, both parts are important:

the objective is carefully defined using loss plus regularization
the algorithm is carefully designed to optimize tree ensembles efficiently
crumbs: Math behind XGBoost

title: Math behind XGBoost
text:
3.14 A summary
We start with a model family \(\mathcal{F}\).
For each candidate function \(f \in \mathcal{F}\), we measure how well it performs using an objective:
\[
\text{obj}(f) = \sum_{i=1}^n l(y_i, f(x_i)) + \Omega(f).
\]
Then learning means solving:
\[
f^\ast = \arg\min_{f \in \mathcal{F}} \text{obj}(f).
\]
This is one of the most important equations in the chapter.
Everything later in XGBoost is a more specific version of this general principle.

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 4.2 2. The model: prediction as a sum of trees
text:
4.2 2. The model: prediction as a sum of trees
Suppose we have training data
\[
(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2), \dots, (x_n, y_n),
\]
where:

\(x_i\) is the feature vector for observation \(i\)
\(y_i\) is the target for observation \(i\)

We want a model that gives a prediction \(\hat y_i\) from \(x_i\).
In linear regression, we often write something like
\[
\hat y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip}.
\]
There, the unknown object is a vector of coefficients \(\beta\).
In XGBoost, the unknown object is not one coefficient vector. Instead, the model is a sum of trees:
\[
\hat y_i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} f_k(x_i), \qquad f_k \in \mathcal{F}.
\]
This formula is the backbone of XGBoost.
It says:

there are \(K\) trees
each tree is a function \(f_k\)
the final prediction is the sum of all tree outputs

So each tree contributes a small correction, and all these corrections accumulate into the final prediction.

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 3.3 3. Why not just build one huge tree?
text:
3.3 3. Why not just build one huge tree?
This is a good question.
If trees are useful, why not build one large, deep tree and be done with it?
Because one huge tree can become unstable and overly sensitive to noise. A very deep tree can fit the training data extremely well, but that does not mean it has learned the real pattern. It may simply have memorized accidental fluctuations.
Boosting takes a different route:

start with a simple model
look at what it still gets wrong
add a new tree that corrects part of that error
repeat gradually

So instead of making one giant jump, boosting makes many small, controlled corrections.
This often leads to a model that is both flexible and well regularized.
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 4.3 3. What exactly is one tree in XGBoost?
text:
4.3 3. What exactly is one tree in XGBoost?
Mathematically, a tree is a function that assigns each input to a leaf, and each leaf has a numerical output.
XGBoost writes a tree as
\[
f(x) = w_{q(x)}.
\]
This compact notation is very important. Let us decode it carefully.
The function \(q(x)\) tells us which leaf the sample \(x\) lands in. If the tree has \(T\) leaves, then \(q(x)\) takes values in \(\{1,2,\dots,T\}\).
The number \(w_j\) is the score assigned to leaf \(j\).
So if a sample \(x\) lands in leaf 3, then
\[
q(x) = 3
\]
and the tree output is
\[
f(x) = w_3.
\]
This means that all observations falling into the same leaf receive exactly the same tree output.
So a tree has two mathematical parts:

a structure, which decides who goes to which leaf
a vector of leaf values, which decides what output each leaf gives

This will matter a lot later, because XGBoost needs to optimize both the tree structure and the leaf values

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 3.5 5. The objective function: what does “good” mean?
text:
3.5 5. The objective function: what does “good” mean?
A model is not useful just because it gives predictions. We need a way to measure whether those predictions are good.
XGBoost does this using an objective function:
\[
\mathrm{Obj} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} l(y_i, \hat y_i) + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \Omega(f_k).
\]
This has two parts.
The first part is the data-fitting term:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} l(y_i, \hat y_i).
\]
Here, \(l(y_i, \hat y_i)\) is the loss for observation \(i\). It tells us how bad the prediction \(\hat y_i\) is when the true answer is \(y_i\).
The second part is the regularization term:
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{K} \Omega(f_k).
\]
This penalizes complexity.
So XGBoost is always balancing two goals:

fit the training data well
keep the model from becoming unnecessarily complicated

This is not just a technical detail. It is the reason XGBoost is often more stable than naive boosting.

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
4.5 5. Regularization for a tree
Let’s first have a look at the regularization. XGBoost uses the following regularization term for a tree:
\[
\Omega(f) = \gamma T + \frac{1}{2}\lambda \sum_{j=1}^{T} w_j^2,
\]
where:

\(T\) is the number of leaves
\(w_j\) is the output value of leaf \(j\)
\(\gamma\) penalizes adding leaves
\(\lambda\) penalizes very large leaf outputs

Let us interpret this slowly.
The term \(\gamma T\) says:
If you create more leaves, you pay a cost.
So a split is not automatically good. A split must improve the fit enough to justify the extra complexity.
The term
\[
\frac{1}{2}\lambda \sum_{j=1}^{T} w_j^2
\]
says ff leaf values become very large in magnitude, you also pay a cost.
So XGBoost prefers leaf outputs that are not too extreme.
This means XGBoost regularizes both the shape of the tree and the size of the corrections made by the leaves.

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 3.7 7. Additive learning: one tree at a time
text:
3.7 7. Additive learning: one tree at a time
If the full model is
\[
\hat y_i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} f_k(x_i),
\]
then training all trees jointly would be very difficult.
XGBoost avoids that by learning additively.
At boosting round \(t\), we already have the current prediction
\[
\hat y_i^{(t-1)}.
\]
Then we add one new tree \(f_t\):
\[
\hat y_i^{(t)} = \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i).
\]
Usually we start from
\[
\hat y_i^{(0)} = 0
\]
or from a constant initial score, depending on the loss.
The essential idea is this:
At round \(t\), all previous trees are fixed. The only new thing we are trying to find is the new tree \(f_t\).
So instead of solving one giant optimization problem, we solve many smaller ones.
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
4.7 7. The objective at boosting round \(t\)
At round \(t\), the new prediction is
\[
\hat y_i^{(t)} = \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i).
\]
So the objective becomes
\[
\mathrm{Obj}^{(t)} =
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i)\right)
+
\Omega(f_t)
+
\text{constant}.
\]
You noticed the constat in the formula, this is because all earlier trees are already fixed. Their contributions to the objective do not change while we are fitting the new tree. So for the purpose of optimizing \(f_t\), all terms involving old trees are constants.
This means the round-\(t\) training problem is choose the new tree \(f_t\) that minimizes
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i)\right)
+
\Omega(f_t).
\]
The hard part is that \(f_t\) is a tree.
That means the thing we want to optimize contains:

a discrete structure, because we must choose splits
continuous parameters, because each leaf has a numerical value

The structure part is combinatorial. There are many possible features to split on, many thresholds, many tree shapes.
So we need a way to evaluate candidate trees efficiently.
The trick is instead of optimizing the true loss directly at each step, XGBoost approximates it locally using a second-order Taylor expansion.

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
3.10 10. Taylor expansion: the intuition first
Taylor expansion is often introduced as a formula, but here the intuition matters more than the formula itself.
Suppose we have a smooth function \(F(z)\). We currently sit at some point \(z_0\). Now we ask:
What happens to \(F(z)\) if we move a little bit from \(z_0\)?
Taylor expansion answers:
If the move is small, we can approximate the new function value by combining

the current value
the slope at the current point
the curvature at the current point

The second-order Taylor approximation is
\[
F(z_0 + \Delta)
\approx
F(z_0) + F'(z_0)\Delta + \frac{1}{2}F''(z_0)\Delta^2.
\]
This formula says:

start from the current height
add a linear correction based on the slope
refine it using curvature

Why is this useful?
Because many difficult functions become much easier to work with when we replace them locally by a quadratic approximation. Quadratic expressions are nice: we can minimize them analytically.
That is exactly what XGBoost does.

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 4.9 9. Taylor expansion in the XGBoost setting
text:
4.9 9. Taylor expansion in the XGBoost setting
We said that if we are at some current point and make a small move, then we can approximate the new function value using three local pieces of information:

the current value
the slope
the curvature

XGBoost does exactly this, but here the function is the loss, and the “current point” is the current prediction.
For observation \(i\), the loss at boosting round \(t\) is
\[
l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i)\right).
\]
Let us read this carefully.

\(y_i\) is the true observed outcome
\(\hat y_i^{(t-1)}\) is the current prediction from all previous trees
\(f_t(x_i)\) is the extra correction added by the new tree at round \(t\)

So the new tree does not replace the old prediction. It only adds a small adjustment to it.
That means we can think of the loss as a function of the prediction value, where we are currently sitting at \(\hat y_i^{(t-1)}\) and then taking a small step of size \(f_t(x_i)\).
We therefore expand the loss around the current prediction \(\hat y_i^{(t-1)}\).
Define the first derivative
\[
g_i =
\left.
\frac{\partial l(y_i, \hat y)}{\partial \hat y}
\right|_{\hat y = \hat y_i^{(t-1)}}
\]
and the second derivative
\[
h_i =
\left.
\frac{\partial^2 l(y_i, \hat y)}{\partial \hat y^2}
\right|_{\hat y = \hat y_i^{(t-1)}}.
\]
These two quantities play exactly the same role as in the general Taylor formula.

\(g_i\) is the local slope of the loss with respect to the prediction
\(h_i\) is the local curvature of the loss with respect to the prediction

So:

\(g_i\) tells us whether increasing the prediction would locally increase or decrease the loss
\(h_i\) tells us how sharply that slope itself changes as we move

Using the second-order Taylor expansion, we get
\[
l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i)\right)
\approx
l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)}\right)
+
g_i f_t(x_i)
+
\frac{1}{2} h_i f_t(x_i)^2.
\]
This approximation has the same three-part structure as before.
First,
\[
l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)}\right)
\]
is the current loss value at the current prediction.
Second,
\[
g_i f_t(x_i)
\]
is the linear correction based on the local slope.
Third,
\[
\frac{1}{2} h_i f_t(x_i)^2
\]
is the curvature correction, which refines the linear approximation by accounting for how the slope changes.
So for each observation, XGBoost replaces the original loss by a local quadratic approximation around the current prediction.
It looks complicated but it is just important to remember that because the original loss may be difficult to optimize directly, this local quadratic form is much easier to work with. Once the loss is written this way, XGBoost can derive explicit formulas for leaf weights and for the gain from making a split.






Note





It is important not to think of gradients abstractly.
For one observation \(i\):
\[
g_i
=
\left.
\frac{\partial l(y_i, \hat y)}{\partial \hat y}
\right|_{\hat y = \hat y_i^{(t-1)}}
\]
tells us how the loss changes if we nudge the prediction a little bit.
So \(g_i\) says in which direction should this prediction move to reduce the loss.
If \(g_i\) is positive, increasing the prediction increases the loss locally, so the prediction would prefer to move downward. If \(g_i\) is negative, increasing the prediction decreases the loss locally, so the prediction would prefer to move upward.
The second derivative
\[
h_i
=
\left.
\frac{\partial^2 l(y_i, \hat y)}{\partial \hat y^2}
\right|_{\hat y = \hat y_i^{(t-1)}}
\]
tells us how sharply the loss bends around the current prediction.
So \(h_i\) answers wow cautious should we be when making that move.
If the curvature is high, the loss changes rapidly, so we should usually take a smaller step. If the curvature is lower, a larger step may be acceptable.
So in plain language:

gradient says where to move
Hessian says how carefully to move

This is why XGBoost uses second-order information.



Now we can substitute the Taylor approximation into the round-\(t\) objective gives
\[
\mathrm{Obj}^{(t)}
\approx
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[
l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)}\right)
+
g_i f_t(x_i)
+
\frac{1}{2} h_i f_t(x_i)^2
\right]
+
\Omega(f_t).
\]
The term
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)}\right)
\]
does not depend on the new tree \(f_t\). So for optimization, it is constant and can be dropped.
This leaves the approximate objective
\[
\tilde{\mathrm{Obj}}^{(t)}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[
g_i f_t(x_i)
+
\frac{1}{2} h_i f_t(x_i)^2
\right]
+
\Omega(f_t).
\]

text:
3.13 13. Why the Taylor approximation is such a big deal
Substituting the Taylor approximation into the round-\(t\) objective gives
\[
\mathrm{Obj}^{(t)}
\approx
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[
l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)}\right)
+
g_i f_t(x_i)
+
\frac{1}{2} h_i f_t(x_i)^2
\right]
+
\Omega(f_t).
\]
The term
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)}\right)
\]
does not depend on the new tree \(f_t\). So for optimization, it is constant and can be dropped.
This leaves the approximate objective
\[
\tilde{\mathrm{Obj}}^{(t)}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[
g_i f_t(x_i)
+
\frac{1}{2} h_i f_t(x_i)^2
\right]
+
\Omega(f_t).
\]
This equation is the real engine of XGBoost.
It says:
To decide the new tree, we do not need the full original loss anymore. We only need the first two derivatives of the loss at the current predictions.
That is why the same machinery works for many different loss functions.

section: 3.14 14. A deeper intuition for the Taylor step
text:
3.14 14. A deeper intuition for the Taylor step
This is worth pausing on.
Before Taylor expansion, the new tree affects the loss through a possibly complicated function:
\[
l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i)\right).
\]
After Taylor expansion, the effect of the new tree becomes approximately quadratic in the tree output:
\[
g_i f_t(x_i)
+
\frac{1}{2} h_i f_t(x_i)^2.
\]
Quadratic functions are much easier to optimize than arbitrary loss functions.
So XGBoost is doing something very clever:
At each step, it turns a hard nonlinear optimization problem into a simpler local quadratic optimization problem.
This is one reason XGBoost is both elegant and computationally effective.

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
4.10 10. Plugging in the tree representation
Recall that a tree is written as
\[
f_t(x) = w_{q(x)}.
\]
So for observation \(i\),
\[
f_t(x_i) = w_{q(x_i)}.
\]
Substituting this into the approximate objective gives
\[
\tilde{\mathrm{Obj}}^{(t)}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[
g_i w_{q(x_i)}
+
\frac{1}{2} h_i w_{q(x_i)}^2
\right]
+
\gamma T
+
\frac{1}{2}\lambda \sum_{j=1}^{T} w_j^2.
\]
Now the tree structure appears through \(q(x_i)\), which tells us which leaf each observation belongs to.

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
4.11 11. Grouping observations by leaf
Let
\[
I_j = \{ i \mid q(x_i) = j \}
\]
be the set of observations that fall into leaf \(j\).
Because every observation in leaf \(j\) gets the same output \(w_j\), we can regroup the objective by leaf instead of by observation.
Then
\[
\tilde{\mathrm{Obj}}^{(t)}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{T}
\left[
\left(\sum_{i \in I_j} g_i\right) w_j
+
\frac{1}{2}
\left(\sum_{i \in I_j} h_i\right) w_j^2
\right]
+
\gamma T
+
\frac{1}{2}\lambda \sum_{j=1}^{T} w_j^2.
\]
Now combine the quadratic terms:
\[
\tilde{\mathrm{Obj}}^{(t)}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{T}
\left[
\left(\sum_{i \in I_j} g_i\right) w_j
+
\frac{1}{2}
\left(\sum_{i \in I_j} h_i + \lambda\right) w_j^2
\right]
+
\gamma T.
\]
Define the leaf-level sums
\[
G_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} g_i,
\qquad
H_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} h_i.
\]
Then the objective becomes
\[
\tilde{\mathrm{Obj}}^{(t)}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{T}
\left[
G_j w_j
+
\frac{1}{2}(H_j + \lambda) w_j^2
\right]
+
\gamma T.
\]
So basicaly once the tree structure is fixed, the entire role of the data inside leaf \(j\) is summarized by just two numbers:
\[
G_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} g_i,
\qquad
H_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} h_i.
\]
That means the samples inside a leaf do not matter individually anymore. What matters is only:

their total gradient
their total Hessian

So the whole optimization for the leaf value \(w_j\) depends only on these aggregated quantities.

text:
3.17 17. Why the leaf statistics \(G_j\) and \(H_j\) are so important
This formula reveals something beautiful.
Once the tree structure is fixed, the entire role of the data inside leaf \(j\) is summarized by just two numbers:
\[
G_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} g_i,
\qquad
H_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} h_i.
\]
That means the samples inside a leaf do not matter individually anymore. What matters is only:

their total gradient
their total Hessian

So the whole optimization for the leaf value \(w_j\) depends only on these aggregated quantities.
This is why XGBoost can evaluate tree structures efficiently. Each leaf is summarized by sufficient statistics.

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
4.12 12. Deriving the optimal leaf value
Now suppose the tree structure is fixed. Then the only unknowns are the leaf outputs \(w_1, \dots, w_T\).
Because the objective separates over leaves, we can optimize one leaf at a time.
For leaf \(j\), the relevant part of the objective is
\[
G_j w_j + \frac{1}{2}(H_j + \lambda) w_j^2.
\]
This is a quadratic function of \(w_j\). This is our objective and we need to minimize it to get an optimal value for it.
To minimize it, differentiate with respect to \(w_j\):
\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial w_j}
\left[
G_j w_j + \frac{1}{2}(H_j + \lambda) w_j^2
\right]
=
G_j + (H_j + \lambda) w_j.
\]
Set the derivative equal to zero:
\[
G_j + (H_j + \lambda) w_j = 0.
\]
Solving for \(w_j\) gives
\[
w_j^\ast = - \frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}.
\]
This is the XGBoost leaf-weight formula for signle leaf.The numerator \(G_j\) is the total gradient pressure in the leaf. It tells us the overall direction in which the predictions of the samples in that leaf want to move.
The denominator \(H_j + \lambda\) controls how large that move should be.

\(H_j\) reflects local curvature of the loss
\(\lambda\) adds shrinkage and stabilizes the update

So the leaf output is negative slope divided by curvature






NoteConnection to Newton’s method





In one-dimensional optimization, Newton’s method updates a parameter by
\[
\theta_{\text{new}}
=
\theta_{\text{old}}
-
\frac{\text{gradient}}{\text{Hessian}}.
\]
That is:

move opposite the slope
scale the step by curvature

The XGBoost leaf formula
\[
w_j^\ast = - \frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}
\]
has exactly the same form. So while ordinary gradient boosting is often explained as fitting negative gradients, XGBoost goes further:
It uses second-order information and computes something much closer to a local Newton update.

text:
3.19 19. Interpreting the leaf-weight formula
The formula
\[
w_j^\ast = - \frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}
\]
should not be memorized blindly. It has a very clear meaning.
The numerator \(G_j\) is the total gradient pressure in the leaf. It tells us the overall direction in which the predictions of the samples in that leaf want to move.
The denominator \(H_j + \lambda\) controls how large that move should be.

\(H_j\) reflects local curvature of the loss
\(\lambda\) adds shrinkage and stabilizes the update

So the leaf output is:
negative slope divided by curvature
That is exactly the logic of Newton’s method.
So every leaf in XGBoost is making a small Newton-style correction.

section: 4.13 13. Deriving the score of a fixed tree structure
text:
4.13 13. Deriving the score of a fixed tree structure
Now let us plug the optimal leaf value back into the objective.
For one leaf, the objective contribution is
\[
G_j w_j + \frac{1}{2}(H_j + \lambda) w_j^2.
\]
Insert
\[
w_j^\ast = - \frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}.
\]
The first term becomes
\[
G_j w_j^\ast
=
G_j \left(- \frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}\right)
=
- \frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda}.
\]
The second term becomes
\[
\frac{1}{2}(H_j + \lambda)(w_j^\ast)^2
=
\frac{1}{2}(H_j + \lambda)
\left(
\frac{G_j^2}{(H_j + \lambda)^2}
\right)
=
\frac{1}{2}
\frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda}.
\]
Adding them gives
\[
- \frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda}
+
\frac{1}{2}
\frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda}
=
- \frac{1}{2}
\frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda}.
\]
So each leaf contributes
\[
- \frac{1}{2}
\frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda}.
\]
Therefore the best objective value for a fixed tree structure is
\[
\tilde{\mathrm{Obj}}^\ast
=
-
\frac{1}{2}
\sum_{j=1}^{T}
\frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda}
+
\gamma T.
\]
This is the score of a tree structure and is important because it tells us how to evaluate a proposed tree structure.
If we know:

which samples fall into each leaf
the sum of gradients in each leaf
the sum of Hessians in each leaf

then we can compute
\[
-\frac{1}{2} \sum_{j=1}^{T} \frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda}+\gamma T
\]
and judge how good that tree is. This essentially replaces impurity measures like Gini or entropy.

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
4.14 14. Deriving the split gain formula
Now let us derive the split criterion.
Suppose we currently have one leaf, which we may or may not split.
Let the parent node contain a set of observations with total gradient and Hessian
\[
G = \sum_{i \in I} g_i,
\qquad
H = \sum_{i \in I} h_i.
\]
If we keep it as one leaf, its best contribution is
\[
- \frac{1}{2} \frac{G^2}{H + \lambda}.
\]
Now think we split this node into a left child and a right child.
Let their statistics be
\[
G_L, H_L
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
G_R, H_R.
\]
Because the children partition the parent, we have
\[
G = G_L + G_R,
\qquad
H = H_L + H_R.
\]
After the split, the best contribution becomes
\[
- \frac{1}{2} \frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda}
-
\frac{1}{2} \frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda}.
\]
But making the split increases the number of leaves, so we must pay the complexity penalty \(\gamma\).
Therefore the improvement from the split, called the gain, is
\[
\mathrm{Gain}
=
\frac{1}{2}
\left[
\frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda}
+
\frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda}
-
\frac{(G_L + G_R)^2}{H_L + H_R + \lambda}
\right]
-
\gamma.
\]
This formula has a very natural meaning.
The term
\[
\frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda}
\]
measures how useful the left child is.
The term
\[
\frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda}
\]
measures how useful the right child is.
The term
\[
\frac{(G_L + G_R)^2}{H_L + H_R + \lambda}
\]
measures how useful the parent would be if it stayed unsplit.
So the gain says how much better is it to give the left and right groups separate corrections instead of forcing them to share one correction?
Then we subtract \(\gamma\) because more leaves mean more complexity.
So a split is good only if the improvement in fit is large enough to justify the added complexity.

The term

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
3.25 25. The deepest intuition behind splitting
Imagine a node that contains two kinds of observations.
One group wants its predictions pushed upward. Another group wants its predictions pushed downward.
If we force them into one leaf, they must share one leaf value. That shared value is a compromise.
But if we split them into two leaves, one side can get a positive correction and the other side can get a negative correction.
That usually improves the objective.
So a split is valuable when different subsets of the node are whispering different correction directions.
That is really what split gain measures.

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 3.26 26. Why XGBoost does not use Gini or entropy here
text:
3.26 26. Why XGBoost does not use Gini or entropy here
This is often confusing to students because trees are associated with Gini impurity, entropy, and variance reduction.
But XGBoost is not building ordinary decision trees for direct prediction. It is building trees that optimize an approximate objective derived from the loss.
So the split criterion is not generic tree impurity. It comes directly from the regularized local optimization problem.
That is why the gain formula is so central. It is not an arbitrary choice. It is derived from the objective.

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 4.15 15. The full algorithm for one boosting round
text:
4.15 15. The full algorithm for one boosting round
Now let us summarize exactly what happens in one round of XGBoost.

4.15.1 Step 1: compute current predictions
Using all trees built so far, compute
\[
\hat y_i^{(t-1)}
\]
for every training observation.


4.15.2 Step 2: compute gradients and Hessians
For each observation, compute
\[
g_i =
\left.
\frac{\partial l(y_i, \hat y)}{\partial \hat y}
\right|_{\hat y = \hat y_i^{(t-1)}}
\]
and
\[
h_i =
\left.
\frac{\partial^2 l(y_i, \hat y)}{\partial \hat y^2}
\right|_{\hat y = \hat y_i^{(t-1)}}.
\]


4.15.3 Step 3: start with a root node
Initially, all observations are in one root node.


4.15.4 Step 4: consider candidate splits
For each feature and each candidate threshold:

split the samples into left and right
compute \(G_L, H_L, G_R, H_R\)
compute the gain

\[
\mathrm{Gain}
=
\frac{1}{2}
\left[
\frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda}
+
\frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda}
-
\frac{(G_L + G_R)^2}{H_L + H_R + \lambda}
\right]
-
\gamma.
\]


4.15.5 Step 5: choose the best split
Select the split with the largest positive gain.
If no split has positive enough gain, stop splitting that node.


4.15.6 Step 6: continue recursively
Repeat the same procedure for child nodes until stopping conditions are met.


4.15.7 Step 7: assign leaf values
Once the tree structure is fixed, compute for each leaf \(j\)
\[
G_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} g_i,
\qquad
H_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} h_i,
\]
and assign the leaf output
\[
w_j^\ast = - \frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}.
\]


4.15.8 Step 8: update the predictions
The new tree outputs
\[
f_t(x_i) = w_{q(x_i)},
\]
and the predictions become
\[
\hat y_i^{(t)}
=
\hat y_i^{(t-1)} + \eta f_t(x_i),
\]
where \(\eta\) is the learning rate.
Then the next boosting round begins.
crumbs: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
3.28 28. Where the learning rate enters
So far, the optimal leaf value is
\[
w_j^\ast = - \frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}.
\]
But XGBoost usually does not apply this full update directly. Instead it uses shrinkage:
\[
\hat y_i^{(t)}
=
\hat y_i^{(t-1)} + \eta f_t(x_i),
\qquad 0 < \eta \le 1.
\]
This means the new tree is scaled by a learning rate \(\eta\).
Why do this?
Because smaller steps often generalize better. Instead of correcting everything aggressively in one round, the model improves gradually.
So:

the leaf formula gives the best local correction
the learning rate says how much of that correction we actually apply
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
3.29 29. Squared-error loss: deriving \(g_i\) and \(h_i\)
Let us now make this concrete.
Suppose the loss is squared error:
\[
l(y_i, \hat y_i) = (y_i - \hat y_i)^2.
\]
Differentiate with respect to \(\hat y_i\):
\[
g_i
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial \hat y_i}
(y_i - \hat y_i)^2
=
2(\hat y_i - y_i).
\]
Differentiate again:
\[
h_i
=
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \hat y_i^2}
(y_i - \hat y_i)^2
=
2.
\]
So for squared loss:

gradient is twice the signed residual
Hessian is a constant

Then for a leaf \(j\),
\[
G_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} 2(\hat y_i - y_i),
\qquad
H_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} 2 = 2|I_j|.
\]
So the leaf value becomes
\[
w_j^\ast
=
-
\frac{\sum_{i \in I_j} 2(\hat y_i - y_i)}{2|I_j| + \lambda}.
\]
If \(\lambda = 0\), then
\[
w_j^\ast
=
\frac{\sum_{i \in I_j} (y_i - \hat y_i)}{|I_j|}.
\]
This is simply the average residual in that leaf.
So the usual story that boosting fits residuals is not wrong. It is just a special case of the more general second-order derivation.
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
3.30 30. Logistic loss: the classification case
Now consider binary classification.
Let the tree ensemble predict a raw score \(s_i\), and convert it to probability using the logistic function
\[
p_i = \sigma(s_i) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-s_i}}.
\]
For binary labels \(y_i \in \{0,1\}\), the logistic loss can be written in a form whose derivatives with respect to the raw score give
\[
g_i = p_i - y_i
\]
and
\[
h_i = p_i(1 - p_i).
\]
This is very important.
For binary classification, XGBoost does not build trees directly on probabilities. It builds trees on the raw score, and the gradients and Hessians are computed with respect to that raw score.
Then the rest of the XGBoost machinery is unchanged:

sum gradients and Hessians inside leaves
compute leaf values
compute split gains
add the new tree to the raw score

So the framework is the same. Only the derivatives change.
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 3.31 31. Why classification and regression fit into the same math
text:
3.31 31. Why classification and regression fit into the same math
This is one of the most elegant parts of XGBoost.
The tree-building machinery does not really care whether the task is regression or classification.
What it needs is:

a loss function
the first derivative of the loss with respect to the current prediction
the second derivative of the loss with respect to the current prediction

Once those are available, the rest of the derivation goes through exactly the same way.
That is why XGBoost is so flexible.
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 3.32 32. A more intuitive look at the Hessian
text:
3.32 32. A more intuitive look at the Hessian
Students often accept gradients fairly quickly but remain unsure about the Hessian.
So let us make it more intuitive.
Imagine the loss as a curve. The gradient tells the slope at the current point.
But slope alone is not always enough.
Suppose two places have the same slope. At one place, the curve bends sharply. At another place, the curve is flatter.
If the curve bends sharply, taking a large step can overshoot. If the curve is flatter, a larger step may be fine.
The Hessian measures this local bending.
So in XGBoost, the Hessian says:
How much trust should I place in the gradient when turning it into a correction?
That is why it appears in the denominator of the leaf formula.
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 3.33 33. A more intuitive look at Taylor expansion
text:
3.33 33. A more intuitive look at Taylor expansion
The Taylor approximation can also be understood as a local surrogate model.
The true loss may be complicated. But near the current prediction, we replace it by a quadratic approximation that has the same:

value
slope
curvature

at the current point.
So we are saying:
I will not try to optimize the full loss globally in one step. I will optimize a faithful local approximation around where I currently am.
That is a very powerful optimization strategy.
It is also why boosting works naturally with many small updates: each new tree is chosen to improve the objective locally.
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
3.34 34. Why the approximation is reasonable
A natural question is:
Why is it okay to use Taylor approximation at all?
The answer is not that it is exact. It is that it is locally informative.
At round \(t\), the new tree is a correction to the current model. If those corrections are not too extreme, then the second-order expansion around the current prediction is often good enough to guide optimization well.
This is especially sensible when:

learning rates are small
trees are not making huge uncontrolled jumps
regularization is active

So XGBoost is not claiming that the Taylor expansion gives the exact global objective. It is using it as a local guide for choosing a good next step.
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 3.35 35. Why the regularization terms matter in practice
text:
3.35 35. Why the regularization terms matter in practice
The two main regularization parameters in the derivation are \(\gamma\) and \(\lambda\).
The parameter \(\gamma\) enters the split gain:
\[
\mathrm{Gain}
=
\frac{1}{2}
\left[
\frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda}
+
\frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda}
-
\frac{(G_L + G_R)^2}{H_L + H_R + \lambda}
\right]
-
\gamma.
\]
So if \(\gamma\) is larger, a split must work harder to be accepted.
This means:

larger \(\gamma\) leads to fewer splits
smaller \(\gamma\) makes the model more willing to grow the tree

The parameter \(\lambda\) enters the leaf formula:
\[
w_j^\ast = - \frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}.
\]
So if \(\lambda\) is larger, leaf values shrink more strongly toward zero.
This means:

larger \(\lambda\) makes updates more conservative
smaller \(\lambda\) allows more aggressive leaf corrections

So \(\gamma\) mainly controls structural complexity, while \(\lambda\) mainly controls the size of leaf outputs.
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 3.36 36. What a leaf is really doing
text:
3.36 36. What a leaf is really doing
A common misunderstanding is to think a leaf is predicting the target directly.
That is not the best way to think about it in boosting.
A leaf is really producing a correction to the current prediction.
If a leaf gets a positive value, then all observations in that leaf have their current predictions moved upward. If a leaf gets a negative value, then their current predictions are moved downward.
So leaves in boosting are not final answers. They are local update rules.
This is why a deep understanding of XGBoost is really a story about iterative correction.
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
3.37 37. A small conceptual example
Suppose a node contains observations whose gradients are mixed.
Some have negative gradients, meaning the prediction is too low and should move upward. Others have positive gradients, meaning the prediction is too high and should move downward.
If we keep them together in one leaf, the best leaf value will average these conflicting pressures.
That may be mediocre.
If we split them into two groups that are more homogeneous in what they want, then each child can receive a more appropriate correction.
This is why splitting reduces the objective. It allows different groups of observations to get different Newton-style updates.
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 3.38 38. The XGBoost story in one continuous flow
text:
3.38 38. The XGBoost story in one continuous flow
At this point, we can tell the whole story from beginning to end.
We want to build a predictive model as a sum of trees:
\[
\hat y_i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} f_k(x_i).
\]
We define an objective that balances loss and complexity:
\[
\mathrm{Obj} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} l(y_i, \hat y_i) + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \Omega(f_k).
\]
At each boosting round, we add one new tree:
\[
\hat y_i^{(t)} = \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i).
\]
Because optimizing the exact objective for a tree is hard, we approximate the change in loss using a second-order Taylor expansion:
\[
l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i)\right)
\approx
l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)}\right)
+
g_i f_t(x_i)
+
\frac{1}{2} h_i f_t(x_i)^2.
\]
This gives an approximate objective
\[
\tilde{\mathrm{Obj}}^{(t)}
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
\left[
g_i f_t(x_i)
+
\frac{1}{2} h_i f_t(x_i)^2
\right]
+
\Omega(f_t).
\]
We express the tree as
\[
f_t(x) = w_{q(x)},
\]
group observations by leaf, and obtain
\[
\tilde{\mathrm{Obj}}^{(t)}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{T}
\left[
G_j w_j + \frac{1}{2}(H_j + \lambda) w_j^2
\right]
+
\gamma T.
\]
From this we derive the optimal leaf value
\[
w_j^\ast = - \frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}
\]
and the score of a fixed structure
\[
\tilde{\mathrm{Obj}}^\ast
=
-
\frac{1}{2}
\sum_{j=1}^{T}
\frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda}
+
\gamma T.
\]
Comparing parent and children gives the split gain
\[
\mathrm{Gain}
=
\frac{1}{2}
\left[
\frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda}
+
\frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda}
-
\frac{(G_L + G_R)^2}{H_L + H_R + \lambda}
\right]
-
\gamma.
\]
That is the mathematical heart of XGBoost.

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 3.39 39. The main formulas collected in one place
text:
3.39 39. The main formulas collected in one place
For quick review, the essential formulas are these.
Model:
\[
\hat y_i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} f_k(x_i)
\]
Additive update:
\[
\hat y_i^{(t)} = \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i)
\]
Tree representation:
\[
f_t(x) = w_{q(x)}
\]

\[
\Omega(f) = \gamma T + \frac{1}{2}\lambda \sum_{j=1}^{T} w_j^2

\[
g_i =
\left.
\frac{\partial l(y_i, \hat y)}{\partial \hat y}
\right|_{\hat y = \hat y_i^{(t-1)}}

\[

\left.
\frac{\partial^2 l(y_i, \hat y)}{\partial \hat y^2}
\right|_{\hat y = \hat y_i^{(t-1)}}
\]

\[
l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i)\right)
\approx
l\left(y_i, \hat y_i^{(t-1)}\right)
+
g_i f_t(x_i)
+
\frac{1}{2} h_i f_t(x_i)^2
\]

\[
G_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} g_i,
\qquad
H_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} h_i
\]
Approximate objective by leaf:
\[
\tilde{\mathrm{Obj}}^{(t)}
=
\sum_{j=1}^{T}
\left[
G_j w_j + \frac{1}{2}(H_j + \lambda) w_j^2
\right]
+
\gamma T
\]
Optimal leaf value:
\[
w_j^\ast = - \frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}
\]
Score of a fixed tree structure:
\[
\tilde{\mathrm{Obj}}^\ast
=
-
\frac{1}{2}
\sum_{j=1}^{T}
\frac{G_j^2}{H_j + \lambda}
+
\gamma T
\]
Split gain:
\[
\mathrm{Gain}
=
\frac{1}{2}
\left[
\frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda}
+
\frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda}
-
\frac{(G_L + G_R)^2}{H_L + H_R + \lambda}
\right]
-
\gamma
\]
Prediction update with learning rate:
\[

\]

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 3.40 40. The one-sentence intuition for each symbol
text:
3.40 40. The one-sentence intuition for each symbol
Here is a compact interpretation of the main symbols.
\(x_i\) is the feature vector of observation \(i\).
\(y_i\) is the true target.
\(\hat y_i\) is the current prediction.
\(f_t\) is the new tree added at boosting round \(t\).
\(q(x)\) tells which leaf a sample lands in.
\(w_j\) is the output assigned to leaf \(j\).
\(g_i\) tells which way the loss wants prediction \(i\) to move.
\(h_i\) tells how sharply the loss bends around prediction \(i\).
\(G_j\) is the total gradient pressure inside leaf \(j\).
\(H_j\) is the total curvature inside leaf \(j\).
\(\lambda\) shrinks leaf outputs.
\(\gamma\) penalizes creating more leaves.
\(\eta\) shrinks the contribution of the whole new tree.
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 3.41 41. The deepest intuition of the whole method
text:
3.41 41. The deepest intuition of the whole method
Every observation speaks to the algorithm through two numbers:

a gradient, which says how its current prediction should change
a Hessian, which says how confident or cautious that change should be

A leaf gathers these local messages from many observations and turns them into one shared correction:
\[
w_j^\ast = - \frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}.
\]
A split is good when one shared correction is not enough, and two separate corrections fit the observations better.
So XGBoost is not mysterious at all. It is an iterative optimization method that uses trees to organize local Newton-style corrections.
crumbs: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
3.42 42. Final summary
If we strip XGBoost down to its mathematical core, it is doing exactly this:

write the model as a sum of trees
define a regularized objective
add one new tree at a time
approximate the loss locally using a second-order Taylor expansion
use gradients and Hessians as local summaries of what the loss wants
derive the best leaf values analytically
derive the best splits by comparing the objective before and after splitting
repeat many times with shrinkage

So the real secret of XGBoost is not a mysterious tree trick. It is the combination of three ideas:

additive boosting
second-order optimization
regularized tree construction

That combination is what makes XGBoost both mathematically elegant and practically powerful.

title: 3  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
3.43 43. What should come next
The best next chapter after this one is usually one of these two:

a fully worked numerical example with a tiny dataset, where we manually compute:

current predictions
gradients
Hessians
one candidate split
leaf values
gain

a separate derivation chapter for specific losses:

squared-error regression
logistic binary classification


Those two sections usually make the whole theory click permanently.

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
4.4 4. The objective function:
As it should be obvious, we also need a way to measure whether our predictions are good or not. XGBoost does this using an objective function:
\[
\mathrm{Obj} = \sum_{i=1}^{n} l(y_i, \hat y_i) + \sum_{k=1}^{K} \Omega(f_k).
\]
This has two parts. The first part is the data-fitting term:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n} l(y_i, \hat y_i).
\]
Here, \(l(y_i, \hat y_i)\) is the loss for observation \(i\). It tells us how bad the prediction \(\hat y_i\) is when the true answer is \(y_i\).
The second part is the regularization term:
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{K} \Omega(f_k).
\]
This penalizes complexity.
So XGBoost is always balancing two goals:

fit the training data well
keep the model from becoming unnecessarily complicated
crumbs: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
4.6 6. Additive learning
If the full model is
\[
\hat y_i = \sum_{k=1}^{K} f_k(x_i),
\]
then training all trees jointly would be very difficult becuase we have to both fix the structure of the tree and its values.
XGBoost avoids that by learning additively.
At boosting round \(t\), we already have the current prediction
\[
\hat y_i^{(t-1)}.
\]
Then we add one new tree \(f_t\):
\[
\hat y_i^{(t)} = \hat y_i^{(t-1)} + f_t(x_i).
\]
Usually we start from
\[
\hat y_i^{(0)} = 0
\]
or from a constant initial score, depending on the loss.
The essential idea is that at round \(t\), all previous trees are fixed. The only new thing we are trying to find is the new tree \(f_t\). So instead of solving one giant optimization problem, we solve many smaller ones.
crumbs: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
4.8 8. Taylor expansion
Suppose we have a smooth function \(F(z)\), and we are currently at the point \(z_0\).
What happens to the value of the function if we move a little away from \(z_0\)?
Let that small move be \(\Delta\). Then the new point is \(z_0 + \Delta\).
Taylor expansion gives us a very useful local approximation. It says that if the move is small, then we do not need to know the full complicated shape of the function. We only need to know three things at the current point:

the current value of the function
the current slope
the current curvature

Using those three pieces of information, we can approximate the new function value as
\[
F(z_0 + \Delta)
\approx
F(z_0) + F'(z_0)\Delta + \frac{1}{2}F''(z_0)\Delta^2.
\]
First, \(F(z_0)\) is the value of the function where we are right now. That is our starting point.
Next, \(F'(z_0)\Delta\) is the linear correction. The first derivative (\(F'(z_0)\)) tells us whether the function is currently going up or down, and how steeply. So this term tells us how the function would change if the slope stayed roughly constant for a very small move.
Finally, \(\frac{1}{2}F''(z_0)\Delta^2\) adds a curvature correction. The second derivative (\(F''(z_0)\)) tells us how the slope itself changes as we move.

If (\(F''(z_0) > 0\)), the curve bends upward.
If (\(F''(z_0) < 0\)), the curve bends downward.
If (\(F''(z_0) \approx 0\)), the function is locally almost straight.

So the second derivative tells us whether the current trend is becoming stronger or weaker as we move away from (\(z_0\)).
This is why the Taylor approximation is so useful. Even if the original function is complicated, near the current point it can be approximated by a quadratic expression. Quadratic expressions are much easier to optimize, because we can minimize them analytically.

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
text:
4.16 16. A bit about learning rate
So far, the optimal leaf value is
\[
w_j^\ast = - \frac{G_j}{H_j + \lambda}.
\]
But XGBoost usually does not apply this full update directly. Instead it uses shrinkage:
\[
\hat y_i^{(t)}
=
\hat y_i^{(t-1)} + \eta f_t(x_i),
\qquad 0 < \eta \le 1.
\]
This means the new tree is scaled by a learning rate \(\eta\). Because smaller steps often generalize better. Instead of correcting everything aggressively in one round, the model improves gradually.

title: 4  Math behind XGBoost: from scratch, slowly, and with intuition
section: 4.17 Special case. Squared-error loss: deriving \(g_i\) and \(h_i\)
text:
4.17 Special case. Squared-error loss: deriving \(g_i\) and \(h_i\)
Suppose the loss is squared error:
\[
l(y_i, \hat y_i) = (y_i - \hat y_i)^2.
\]
Differentiate with respect to \(\hat y_i\):
\[
g_i
=
\frac{\partial}{\partial \hat y_i}
(y_i - \hat y_i)^2
=
2(\hat y_i - y_i).
\]
Differentiate again:
\[
h_i
=
\frac{\partial^2}{\partial \hat y_i^2}
(y_i - \hat y_i)^2
=
2.
\]
So for squared loss:

gradient is twice the signed residual
Hessian is a constant

Then for a leaf \(j\),
\[
G_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} 2(\hat y_i - y_i),
\qquad
H_j = \sum_{i \in I_j} 2 = 2|I_j|.
\]
So the leaf value becomes
\[
w_j^\ast
=
-
\frac{\sum_{i \in I_j} 2(\hat y_i - y_i)}{2|I_j| + \lambda}.
\]
If \(\lambda = 0\), then
\[
w_j^\ast
=
\frac{\sum_{i \in I_j} (y_i - \hat y_i)}{|I_j|}.
\]
This is simply the average residual in that leaf.
So if you hear that boosting fits residuals, this is not wrong. it’s just a special case of squared error loss.

title: 2  How to model using XGBoost
text:
13.1 1. Regression
Use these when the outcome is numerical.

objective = "reg:squarederror"
This is the standard choice for ordinary regression. A very natural metric is rmse, since it is on the same scale as the outcome and is easy to interpret. Another reasonable option is mae if you want a metric that is less sensitive to large errors.
objective = "reg:absoluteerror"
This is useful when you want training to focus on absolute errors rather than squared errors. A sensible metric here is mae. You can still monitor rmse too, but mae usually matches the training goal more directly.
objective = "reg:squaredlogerror"
This can be useful when large target values should not dominate the fit too much, or when relative errors matter more than absolute ones. The most natural metric is rmsle. This setup requires care because the log transformation imposes restrictions on the predictions.
objective = "count:poisson"
Use this for count outcomes, such as numbers of events. A sensible default metric is poisson-nloglik, since it matches the count-model likelihood.
objective = "survival:cox"
Use this for right-censored survival data when you want a Cox proportional hazards type model. A natural metric is cox-nloglik.

A practical starting point for most ordinary regression tasks is:
param <- list(
  objective = "reg:squarederror",
  eval_metric = "rmse"
)

title: 2  How to model using XGBoost
text:
13.2 2. Binary classification
Use these when the outcome has two classes, such as yes/no, case/control, or disease/no disease.

objective = "binary:logistic" This is usually the best default for binary classification because it outputs probabilities. Very common metrics are logloss and auc. Use logloss when you care about well-calibrated probabilities, and auc when you mainly care about ranking positives above negatives. If you want an error rate at a fixed cutoff, you can also monitor error.
objective = "binary:hinge" This gives hard class labels directly instead of probabilities. In that case, error is the most natural metric.

A strong default for most binary problems is:
param <- list(
  objective = "binary:logistic",
  eval_metric = "logloss"
)
If class ranking is especially important, this is also common:
param <- list(
  objective = "binary:logistic",
  eval_metric = "auc"
)
crumbs: 2  How to model using XGBoost

title: 2  How to model using XGBoost
text:
13.3 3. Multiclass classification
Use these when there are more than two classes.

objective = "multi:softprob" This is usually the most flexible choice because it returns class probabilities for all classes. The most sensible metrics are mlogloss and merror. mlogloss is usually better for training and early stopping because it uses the full probability information, while merror is easier to explain as plain misclassification rate. You must also specify num_class.
objective = "multi:softmax" This outputs only the predicted class label, not the full class probabilities. A natural metric here is merror. This is fine if you only care about the final class call, but multi:softprob is often more useful in practice because you can still convert probabilities to class labels later.

A good default is:
param <- list(
  objective = "multi:softprob",
  eval_metric = "mlogloss",
  num_class = 3
)
crumbs: 2  How to model using XGBoost

title: 2  How to model using XGBoost
text:
13.4 4. Ranking
Use these when the goal is to rank items rather than predict a simple class or number, such as search results or recommendation lists.

objective = "rank:ndcg" A natural metric is ndcg.
objective = "rank:map" A natural metric is map.
objective = "rank:pairwise" This is another common ranking objective, often monitored with ndcg or map depending on the problem.
crumbs: 2  How to model using XGBoost

title: 2  How to model using XGBoost
text:
13.5 A simple rule of thumb
A good practical rule is: choose an eval_metric that matches the thing you truly care about on unseen data.

If you care about average prediction error in regression, use rmse or mae.
If you care about probability quality in classification, use logloss or mlogloss.
If you care about ranking positives above negatives, use auc.
If you care about plain classification accuracy, use error or merror, but be careful because these can hide important problems such as class imbalance.
